paras: The attempted lynching of Frank Brown took place in Muscatine, Iowa, on the night of March 28, 1903, when a crowd chased, beat and tried to lynch Brown, a Black man who had shot a white man who struck him. Police and an armed guard held off the crowd on the street and at the jail. The wounded man recovered, and in late April Brown was released when the county attorney moved to dismiss the charge as self-defense.

Brown had come to Muscatine from Des Moines and worked for a physician, Dr. F. H. Little. A Muscatine special to the Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican said he stood out for his fine clothes, cane and flat hat, and traced the shooting to remarks about his dress, which he resented.

At about 8 o'clock on Saturday evening, March 28, Brown came out of a store and met Holzhauer, who struck him; the Argus said Holzhauer had been waiting outside for him. Brown drew a revolver and shot Holzhauer in the chest, then ran, firing once at a pursuing policeman without effect.

Within minutes a crowd, joined by Holzhauer's friends, gave chase. In the wire account, the civilians outran the police and about twenty men beat Brown with their fists until twenty policemen charged them with clubs and revolvers and took him away. Local versions differ: one says he was cornered in a drug store and gave up his revolver, the other that a private detective named Zeug captured him and handed him to Officers Thurman and Ziffren.

On the way to jail the police had to keep beating back the crowd, which shouted "Lynch the black" and "String him to a telephone pole." After Brown was locked in a cell, the crowd tried to break into the jail but was stopped by a special force of armed men, and Holzhauer's friends said they would lynch him as soon as they could reach him. On Sunday morning "gangs of toughs from South Muscatine" gathered around the jail amid many threats of lynching, and Sheriff Stuart said he would protect the prisoner at any cost.

By April 3 Holzhauer's physicians said he would recover, and Brown, charged with attempt to commit murder, waived a preliminary hearing so that his case could go to the grand jury; his friends hired lawyers. On about April 24 he was freed: the Ottumwa Semi-Weekly Courier reported that he was "acquitted" for lack of convicting testimony, and the Iowa State Bystander that the county attorney moved to dismiss the case as self-defense. No arrest of anyone in the crowd was reported.

The story reached the white press through a wire dated Muscatine, March 28, which ran the next day in the Omaha Daily Bee as "IOWA POLICE JUST SAVE NEGRO" and in the Indianapolis Journal, whose headline added that the would-be lynchers had "Stoned the Jail." On March 30 it ran as far away as Augusta, Maine ("MOB OF 1500") and St. Paul ("IOWA NEGRO BEATEN SEVERELY BY A MOB"), and an Iowa weekly reprinted it on April 8.

Papers nearer Muscatine showed more sympathy: the Times-Republican called the cause "trivial," and the Rock Island Argus said Brown was "assaulted by the white man, who was waiting for him outside." When Brown was freed, the Ottumwa paper headlined the item "ALLEGED MURDERER FREED."

The Black weekly Iowa State Bystander treated Brown as a known member of its community. On April 3 it reported that his friends "of this city" were sorry to hear of the shooting, called him "a very quick and unassuming young man," and stressed that the other man struck him first. Reporting his release on April 24, it said he had come "very near being lynched" by "some of the Muscatine's unreasonable men" and would doubtless have been lynched "if he had been in the South."

Accounts differ on the capture: only the wire reports that Brown was beaten, while the Muscatine special and the Argus describe officers holding a crowd of 1,500 or 2,000 off as they took him to jail. Early reports called Holzhauer fatally wounded, but the Argus doubted it and his doctors later said he would recover.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Brown
bases: A crowd caught and beat Brown and, by every account, sought to lynch him on the street and at the jail until police and an armed guard stopped it, so this is an attempted lynching (A1, A5, A7, A17).

The press wire (A1), two separate Times-Republican specials from Muscatine (A4, A5), the Rock Island Argus (A7) and the Black Iowa State Bystander (A14, A17) independently agree that Brown shot Holzhauer after being struck and narrowly escaped lynching.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Holtzhauer struck Brown in the face during a quarrel; Brown shot him; civilians outran the police, caught Brown and a score beat him until twenty policemen charged with clubs and revolvers; the mob then tried to break into the jail and Holtzhauer's friends vowed to lynch him.

accounts.label: Times-Republican Muscatine specials
accounts.gist: Brown was cornered in a drug store by a mob of 1,500 and surrendered his revolver; police repeatedly beat back the mob on the way to jail; the quarrel grew out of remarks about Brown's fine dress, which he resented.

accounts.label: Rock Island Argus
accounts.gist: Holzhauer, after earlier trouble, waited outside a clothing store and assaulted Brown; a private detective captured him and officers had great difficulty preventing a lynching by 2,000 people.

accounts.label: Iowa State Bystander
accounts.gist: The man struck Brown a severe blow before Brown shot him; the county attorney later moved to dismiss as self-defense, and the paper said Brown nearly was lynched by 'unreasonable men'.

framing.detail: The wire, under headlines such as 'IOWA POLICE JUST SAVE NEGRO' and 'MOB OF 1500', told the story as a narrow rescue and reported, without comment, the vow of Holtzhauer's friends to lynch Brown.
The Times-Republican called the cause 'trivial' and described Brown as 'a real aristocrat' with a cane and fine clothes, while noting feeling abated once he told his story.
The Rock Island Argus said Brown was 'assaulted by the white man, who was waiting for him outside' and headlined that he 'BARELY ESCAPES BEING LYNCHED'.
The Iowa State Bystander blamed 'Muscatine's unreasonable men' and said he would doubtless have been lynched in the South.

conflicts.note: Both are round estimates; the Argus figure refers to the crowd on the way to jail.
